body:
Understanding Heat and Temperature

Hot tea cools when left on a table, ice melts in a warm room, and a metal spoon becomes hot when placed in boiling water. These familiar observations involve the transfer of thermal energy. To explain them correctly, it is necessary to distinguish heat from temperature.

Heat

Heat is energy transferred from one body or system to another because of a temperature difference. When two bodies at different temperatures interact thermally, the net transfer of heat occurs from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.

Temperature

Temperature is the physical quantity that indicates the thermal condition of a body and determines the direction of spontaneous heat transfer. It is related to the microscopic motion of the particles constituting matter.

Heat and temperature are therefore related but are not interchangeable. Temperature indicates how hot or cold a body is, whereas heat describes energy transferred because of a temperature difference.

Why Temperature Depends on Particle Motion

All matter consists of particles. In solids, particles mainly vibrate about relatively fixed positions. In liquids, particles can move past one another, while in gases they move comparatively freely.

The particles possess energy because of their motion and interactions. The total microscopic kinetic and potential energy associated with these particles forms the internal energy of the substance.

When a substance is heated without changing its physical state, its temperature generally rises because its particles acquire greater thermal motion. When a substance cools, its thermal motion generally decreases.

Temperature is closely related to average microscopic kinetic energy, particularly for an ideal gas. However, the total internal energy of a substance also depends on the amount and nature of matter and the interactions between its particles.

Why Heat and Temperature Are Different

Consider a cup of water and a large vessel containing water, both at 50°C. Their temperatures are equal, but the larger quantity of water has more internal energy because it contains more matter under otherwise comparable conditions.

Similarly, a small metal object can have a higher temperature than a large quantity of warm water without possessing more total internal energy.

The important distinction is that temperature does not measure the total thermal energy contained in a body.

Direction of Heat Transfer

Suppose a metal spoon at 20°C is placed in tea at 70°C. Heat flows from the tea to the spoon because the tea is hotter. The spoon becomes warmer while the tea loses some energy.

If this system is perfectly insulated from its surroundings and sufficient time is allowed, the spoon and tea approach a common final temperature. That temperature lies between their initial temperatures and depends on their masses and thermal properties.

This final condition is called thermal equilibrium. When 2 bodies are at the same temperature, there is no net heat transfer between them, although microscopic energy exchanges can continue.

The temperature difference determines the direction of spontaneous heat transfer. The amount transferred depends on additional factors, including the quantity of matter, its thermal properties, and the conditions of contact.

Units of Heat and Temperature

Heat is a form of energy transfer, so its SI unit is the joule (J). Larger quantities may be expressed in kilojoules (kJ).

Temperature has the SI unit kelvin (K). Celsius (°C) and Fahrenheit (°F) are also used for temperature measurements.

The calorie is a traditional unit of heat energy. Approximately 1 calorie equals 4.184 joules. It is different from a degree Celsius, which measures temperature.

Why Touch Can Be Misleading

A steel object and a wooden object kept in the same room for a long time may both have a temperature of 25°C. Yet steel often feels colder when touched.

This happens because steel conducts heat away from the warmer hand much faster than wood. The difference in sensation is caused mainly by the rate of heat transfer, not by a difference in the objects' temperatures.

Therefore, the sensation of hotness or coldness cannot always determine temperature accurately. A thermometer provides a more reliable measurement.

Prelims focus

  • Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference.
  • Temperature determines the direction of spontaneous heat transfer.
  • The SI unit of heat is joule; the SI unit of temperature is kelvin.
  • Heat flows spontaneously from higher temperature to lower temperature.
  • At thermal equilibrium, there is no net heat transfer between bodies.
  • Trap: Equal temperatures do not necessarily mean equal internal energies.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 4: Heat, printed pp. 35–40, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 1: Matter in Our Surroundings, printed pp. 1–7, 2018–19 printing.]

title: Heat and Temperature: Meaning, Differences and Heat Flow

body:
Measuring Temperature

A thermometer is an instrument used to measure temperature. Different thermometers operate by detecting a physical property that changes predictably with temperature.

Traditional liquid-in-glass thermometers use the expansion of a liquid such as mercury or coloured alcohol. Many modern digital thermometers use electronic sensors whose electrical properties change with temperature.

Different instruments are designed for different temperature ranges and purposes.

Clinical and Laboratory Thermometers

FeatureTraditional clinical thermometerLaboratory thermometer
PurposeMeasuring human body temperatureMeasuring temperatures of substances
Typical textbook range35°C to 42°CAbout -10°C to 110°C
Traditional mercury designHas a constriction or kink to retain the reading temporarilyUsually has no retaining constriction
Modern alternativesDigital and electronic clinical thermometersDigital probes and other laboratory instruments

These ranges describe common textbook instruments, not universal limits for every thermometer. Modern electronic instruments may have different ranges and features.

The commonly quoted normal human body temperature is approximately 37°C or 98.6°F. It is an average reference value rather than an exact temperature that every healthy person must have at all times.

Three Important Temperature Scales

Celsius Scale

The Celsius scale uses degrees Celsius (°C). Under normal atmospheric pressure, the melting point of pure ice is approximately 0°C and the boiling point of pure water is approximately 100°C.

These familiar reference temperatures are widely used in general-science questions.

Kelvin Scale

Kelvin is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature. Unlike Celsius, kelvin is written without the degree symbol.

The relationship between the Celsius and Kelvin scales is:

\(T_K = T_C + 273.15\)

For approximate school-level calculations, 273 is sometimes used instead of 273.15.

The zero of the Kelvin scale is absolute zero, equal to -273.15°C. Absolute zero is the lower limit of the thermodynamic temperature scale. It should not be interpreted as meaning that every form of microscopic energy disappears.

Fahrenheit Scale

Fahrenheit is another temperature scale. The conversion from Celsius is:

\(T_F = \frac{9}{5}T_C + 32\)

For example, 0°C is equal to 32°F, and 100°C is equal to 212°F.

Reference conditionCelsiusKelvinFahrenheit
Absolute zero-273.15°C0 K-459.67°F
Melting of pure ice at 1 atmosphere0°C273.15 K32°F
Approximate normal body temperature37°C310.15 K98.6°F
Boiling of pure water at 1 atmosphere100°C373.15 K212°F

The freezing and boiling temperatures listed for water apply to pure water under the specified pressure. Changing pressure can change the boiling temperature.

Heat Capacity and Specific Heat Capacity

Different substances do not experience the same temperature rise when they receive equal quantities of heat.

For example, if equal masses of water and iron receive equal amounts of heat, the iron generally experiences a greater temperature rise than water, provided neither changes its physical state.

This difference is explained by specific heat capacity.

Specific heat capacity

The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of that substance by 1°C or 1 K, without a change of physical state.

Its SI unit is joule per kilogram per kelvin, written J/(kg K).

Water has a comparatively high specific heat capacity. This means that a relatively large amount of heat is required to increase its temperature.

Water also releases considerable energy as it cools. This property helps explain why large water bodies generally warm and cool more slowly than nearby land.

Specific heat capacity also explains why water is widely useful as a cooling medium and why oceans and seas moderate temperatures in coastal regions.

Heat Capacity Versus Specific Heat Capacity

Heat capacity describes the heat required to raise the temperature of an entire body by 1°C or 1 K.

Specific heat capacity describes the heat required per kilogram for the same temperature increase.

Thus, heat capacity depends on both the mass and material of a body, whereas specific heat capacity is a property of the material under specified conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Kelvin is the SI unit of temperature.
  • 0°C = 273.15 K = 32°F.
  • 100°C = 373.15 K = 212°F at normal atmospheric pressure.
  • Normal human body temperature is approximately 37°C.
  • Water has a high specific heat capacity compared with many common materials.
  • Trap: A large temperature rise does not necessarily mean that more heat was supplied; mass and specific heat capacity also matter.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 4: Heat, printed pp. 36–40, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 1: Matter in Our Surroundings, printed pp. 6–9, 2018–19 printing; U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School, Specific Heat Capacity and Water, 24 August 2026, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Equal masses of water and iron receive equal heat from the same starting temperature; water warms less because its specific heat capacity is higher.
pictures.caption: Water undergoes a smaller temperature rise than iron for the same heat supplied to equal masses.

title: Measurement of Temperature, Temperature Scales and Specific Heat

body:
How Heat Travels Through a Solid

When one end of a metal rod is heated, the other end gradually becomes warmer. Heat travels through the rod even though the rod as a whole does not move from one place to another.

This mode of heat transfer is called conduction.

Conduction is the transfer of thermal energy through a substance, or between bodies in contact, without bulk movement of the substance itself.

In a solid, particles near the hotter region transfer energy to neighbouring particles through their interactions. In metals, mobile electrons also contribute significantly to thermal conduction.

As a result, energy spreads from the hotter region towards the cooler region.

Good Conductors and Poor Conductors

Materials differ considerably in their ability to conduct heat.

Material categoryCommon examplesThermal behaviour
Good conductorsCopper, aluminium, ironTransfer heat relatively rapidly
Poor conductorsWood, plastic, rubberTransfer heat relatively slowly
Gases under ordinary conditionsAirGenerally conduct heat poorly
Liquids under ordinary conditionsWaterGenerally conduct heat less effectively than common metals

A poor conductor is commonly called a thermal insulator. An insulator slows heat transfer; it does not necessarily stop heat transfer completely.

Why Cooking Utensils Use Different Materials

Many cooking vessels have metal bodies because metals transfer heat efficiently from the heated surface to food.

Copper and aluminium are particularly useful where rapid heat transfer is desirable. A stainless-steel vessel may have a copper or aluminium base to improve heat distribution.

Handles are often made of wood, heat-resistant plastic, or other materials that conduct heat poorly. This reduces the rate at which heat reaches the hand.

However, a handle made from an insulating material can still become hot if exposed to heat for sufficiently long or under unsuitable conditions.

Conduction in Everyday Situations

Suppose a steel spoon and a wooden spoon initially at 25°C are placed in water at 80°C.

Heat passes from the hot water into both spoons. Because steel is a much better thermal conductor than wood, heat travels along the steel spoon more rapidly.

The same principle explains several familiar observations.

  • Metal cooking utensils: Their conducting surfaces help transfer heat to food.
  • Metal door handles: They often feel colder than wooden handles at the same room temperature because they draw heat from the hand more rapidly.
  • Insulated containers: Poorly conducting layers reduce heat exchange between the contents and the surroundings.
  • Metallic heat sinks: Good conductors help carry heat away from components that become warm during operation.

Does Conduction Occur Only in Solids?

No. Conduction can occur in solids, liquids and gases. However, it is generally the dominant mode of heat transfer within a stationary solid.

Liquids and gases can also transport heat by convection, which involves the bulk movement of fluid.

Therefore, a statement claiming that conduction is possible only in solids is incorrect.

Factors Affecting Conduction

The rate of conduction depends on the nature of the material, the temperature difference, the thickness of the material and the area available for heat transfer.

Other conditions being equal, a larger temperature difference generally increases the rate of heat transfer. A thicker insulating layer generally reduces the rate of conduction across it.

These relationships explain why a thick insulating wall slows heat transfer more effectively than a thin wall made from the same material.

Prelims focus

  • Conduction transfers heat without bulk movement of matter.
  • Conduction is generally important in solids.
  • Copper and aluminium are good thermal conductors.
  • Wood, rubber and common plastics are poor conductors.
  • A metal spoon becomes hot through conduction.
  • Trap: Insulators reduce the rate of heat transfer; they do not make heat transfer impossible.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 4: Heat, section 4.4, printed pp. 40–42, 2018–19 printing.]

title: Conduction: Heat Transfer Through Materials
